evaluation.positioning_hook: A CIA trainee with trauma-trained instincts discovers her agency’s reality-warping training system is rewriting her life — and the man she loves may be part of the program.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise has immediate commercial lift: CIA ops, a mind-bending training system, and a romance threaded through espionage give it a clear genre promise. The opening Istanbul snatch, the ARC reveal, and the live D.C. climax all signal a movie with broad thriller appeal and a strong trailer shape.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands early and cleanly: a clandestine training program uses augmented reality to shape operatives, and one recruit starts seeing through it. The Georgetown lecture, the ARC backlot reveal, and the final live-op turn make the engine easy to explain in two sentences.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Ridley is built as a compelling lead: trauma-informed, sharp, resistant to authority, and emotionally legible through her work with victims and her history with West. Ian gives the story a second strong center, and the ensemble trainees each have a functional identity that supports the lead pair.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script’s boldest move is turning intelligence training into a gamified, neural-linked reality layer that can literally overwrite perception. The repeated use of simulation bleed, leaderboard logic, and memory manipulation gives the material a confident, contemporary sci-fi identity.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The script moves with real propulsion from Istanbul to Georgetown to The Farm to the live D.C. op, and each sequence escalates the stakes or reframes what came before. The rooftop climax and the final cycle reveal keep the story in motion and reward the setup.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The core idea feels fresh and inevitable: predictive intelligence training that weaponizes trauma and perception, then collapses into a real-world op. The emotional spine — trust, control, and whether instinct can beat optimization — gives the concept a memorable aftertaste.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The CIA training ecosystem, ARC card system, leaderboard culture, and live-op mirroring create a world with rules and hierarchy, not just a backdrop. The Farm, the backlot overwrites, and the operational language all make the setting feel story-generating.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is distinct: espionage procedural pressure collides with psychological horror, romantic tension, and tech-noir unease. The script can pivot from hand-to-hand action to intimate memory fracture without losing its identity.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: What starts as a training thriller opens into a deeper question about identity, consent, memory, and institutional control. The final cycle reveal and the repeated recontextualization of Ridley’s past give the material a strong sense of hidden architecture.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Ridley/Ian is the engine, and the Ridley/Alvarez/Egan/Denny dynamic adds useful friction and contrast. The ensemble is strong enough to generate multiple pairings and ideological splits, though the story still lives most powerfully through the central duo.

casting_characteristics: Two lead roles with strong chemistry demands
One senator role with authority and public-facing charisma

notable_requirements: International city stand-ins for Istanbul, Paris, Serbia, Yemen, Taipei, Moscow, and London subway environments
Server room, observation room, barracks, medical center, and tactical house interiors

technical.vfx_details: Augmented-reality overlays, HUD graphics, environment overwrites, simulation dissolves, digital face morphing, and data visualization sequences.
technical.sfx_needs: Gunfire, explosions, rooftop falls, vehicle impacts, simulated combat, and practical blood/medical effects.

rights_flags.detail: Senator Robert Kerrigan is a named political figure within the story world.
Apple Watch is referenced by name.
World Bank and IMF are referenced in dialogue.
Collection Deck is referenced as an in-world training game/card system.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model with strong festival-to-platform or streamer-premiere potential; the hook is the espionage thriller engine plus the reality-bending training concept.

cost.note: The story is contemporary and largely contained, but the AR overwrites, multiple international stand-ins, and action set pieces push it above a lean indie budget.

cast.note: The project is anchored by two demanding leads and a manageable ensemble, with no child roles or star-dependent crowd scenes.

location.note: The script moves through many distinct environments and multiple international city looks, including a live D.C. climax and several simulated foreign locales.

content.note: The material includes gun violence, torture-adjacent psychological control, explosions, and intense threat language, but stays within thriller territory.

rights.note: Several named brands and institutions appear in dialogue, plus a named political figure and an in-world game system that may need clearance or fictionalization.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The premise turns training into the battleground.
strengths.what_it_means: That gives the movie a clean commercial engine: every exercise can become a set piece, and every set piece can reveal character while advancing the conspiracy. Buyers who want a high-concept thriller with built-in escalation will see a concept that can sell on premise alone.
strengths.evidence: The ARC backlot overwrite, the dojo fight, the Paris safe house exercise, and the live D.C. op all function as story turns and action sequences.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Ridley is a showcase lead role.
strengths.what_it_means: She can play intelligence, vulnerability, anger, and physical command in the same role, which is exactly the kind of part that can elevate an actor into a prestige-thriller lane. Mid-career actresses looking for a franchise-capable lead with emotional depth and action credibility will chase this.
strengths.evidence: Her Georgetown lecture on coercive control, her instinctive resistance to ARC prompts, and her final choice to override the system all define her as more than a genre function.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The Ian/Ridley dynamic has real heat.
strengths.what_it_means: The script gives the project a romantic and ideological spine, which broadens the audience beyond pure espionage fans and gives marketing a human hook. Actors who can play chemistry under pressure will be drawn to a relationship that is both tender and adversarial.
strengths.evidence: Their bar reunion, the dojo competition, the memory fractures, and the rooftop reunion all build a relationship that matters to the plot and the emotion.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The world has a strong institutional texture.
strengths.what_it_means: The CIA training culture, the card-based intelligence taxonomy, and the leaderboard logic make the setting feel like a system with rules, not just a backdrop. That kind of specificity helps a buyer imagine repeatable story mechanics and a director imagine a visual language.
strengths.evidence: ARC cards for HUMINT, SIGINT, GEOINT, and DIRECT ACTION; the Farm; the observation room; and the live-op mirroring of simulations.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The script has a strong paranoia engine.
strengths.what_it_means: The audience is constantly asked to question what is real, who is controlling whom, and whether the protagonist’s memories can be trusted. That creates the kind of forward-leaning suspense that keeps a thriller sticky after the first watch.
strengths.evidence: West appearing as Dawson, the cycle resets, the memory architecture reveal, and the final acceptance of human override.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The action is concept-driven, not random.
strengths.what_it_means: The fights and chases are tied to the system’s logic, so the action feels story-specific rather than generic. That makes the material more attractive to producers who want spectacle that also advances theme and character.
strengths.evidence: Ridley’s improvised dojo win versus Ian’s system-perfect fight, the rooftop confrontation, and the embassy-row pursuit all reflect the script’s central argument about instinct versus optimization.

whats_special.headline: AGENCY is a sleek, high-concept espionage thriller with a built-in action engine: CIA trainees, reality-warping simulation tech, and a lead heroine whose instincts keep beating the machine. It has the kind of contained-yet-scalable premise that can attract a strong actress, a performance-forward director, and a premium buyer looking for a smart commercial hook.

lead_characters.name: Ridley Cooper
lead_characters.hook: Ridley is a trauma expert who reads people for a living, but the script keeps testing whether she can read herself. She’s smart, guarded, emotionally disciplined, and quietly furious at systems that flatten human complexity into data; that contradiction is the engine of the role.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Jodie Foster in The Silence of the Lambs — a highly intelligent woman whose composure is part armor, part weapon, and whose inner life keeps tightening the screws on the scene. Actors who want a prestige lead that can play intellect, action, and emotional fracture in the same frame will line up for this.

lead_characters.name: Ian Walsh
lead_characters.demographics: Male · mid-20s to early 30s · athletic, operative-trained
lead_characters.hook: Ian is the guy who believes the system can be made better if he just pushes hard enough, which makes him both admirable and dangerous. He’s competitive, charming, and physically precise, but the script gives him a real emotional fault line: the part of him that wants to trust the machine and the part that still remembers how to feel.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase lane of Matthew McConaughey in True Detective — a controlled, charismatic lead whose confidence slowly reveals a haunted interior. Actors who want a role that can play action competence, romantic tension, and ideological collapse will see a lot of runway here.

lead_characters.name: Dawson
lead_characters.hook: Dawson is the smiling interface between policy, tech, and coercion. He’s calm, persuasive, and hard to pin down, which makes him feel like a man who has already decided that human messiness is the thing to be engineered out of the room.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the controlled menace of Michael Shannon in a prestige conspiracy thriller — authority without volume, threat without spectacle. Character actors who like playing intelligence and duplicity in the same breath will be drawn to it.

lead_characters.name: Sykes
lead_characters.hook: Sykes is the old-school operator who speaks in orders and consequences. He’s not flashy, but he gives the story institutional gravity and a clear face for the machine’s moral logic.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets a veteran actor do what Tommy Lee Jones does in political thrillers: compress authority, fatigue, and menace into a few lines. Seasoned character actors who can make command feel lived-in will want it.

lead_characters.name: Harrison
lead_characters.hook: Harrison is the hard-edged trainer who knows how to sell the dream while enforcing the discipline. He’s part mentor, part gatekeeper, and part believer in the system’s promise.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the grounded command of J.K. Simmons in a pressure-cooker institutional drama — a man who can turn a briefing into a scene. Strong supporting players who specialize in authority with bite will chase it.

lead_characters.name: Bill Harrison
lead_characters.hook: Bill is the quieter, deadlier version of institutional competence. He reads as someone who has spent a lifetime turning chaos into procedure and never once apologized for it.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of contained authority role that lets a veteran actor do the understated menace of Bryan Cranston in a procedural thriller. It’s a clean fit for actors who can make expertise feel dangerous.

lead_characters.name: Alvarez
lead_characters.hook: Alvarez is the smartest person in the room who doesn’t need the room to know it. She’s observant, dry, and emotionally self-protective, and she becomes the story’s clearest voice for ambiguity without surrendering competence.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of supporting role that gives an actor the sharp, scene-stealing intelligence of Sarah Snook in Succession — fast thinking, dry wit, and emotional precision. Actors who want a smart, playable role with real utility in the ensemble will want this.

lead_characters.name: Matt Egan
lead_characters.hook: Egan is the guy ARC loves because he loves ARC back. He’s cocky, competitive, and increasingly frightening in the way he treats violence like proof of worth.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Jack O’Connell in a military or prison drama — a volatile, physical role that can turn charisma into menace in a heartbeat. Actors who want to play the seductive danger of overconfidence will chase it.

lead_characters.name: Wyatt Denny
lead_characters.hook: Denny is the nervous systems guy in a room full of people trying to become weapons. He’s thoughtful, reactive, and increasingly rattled by what the system is teaching everyone to ignore.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the anxious intelligence of Paul Dano in a pressure-cooker ensemble — the person who notices the moral cost before everyone else does. Supporting players who can make panic feel human will be drawn to it.

lead_characters.name: Chris Williams
lead_characters.hook: Williams is the quiet one whose mind is always somewhere else, until the system stops letting him leave. He becomes the story’s clearest example of what happens when the machine keeps feeding fear back into itself.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the destabilized intensity of Barry Keoghan in a psychological thriller — a slow turn from contained to overwhelmed. It’s a strong fit for actors who can play internal fracture without over-explaining it.

lead_characters.name: Senator Robert Kerrigan
lead_characters.hook: Kerrigan is the political face of the guardrails argument, and the script smartly gives him personal stakes through grief. He’s not just a speechmaker; he’s a man trying to stop a system he understands too well.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives a veteran actor the moral authority of Jeff Daniels in a political thriller — public composure with private damage underneath. Prestige character actors who can make a speech feel like a scene will want it.

director_appeal.hook: A director who wants to make a sleek paranoia thriller with a strong visual system and emotional stakes.
director_appeal.fit_profile: Second- or third-feature directors, or established indie directors moving into elevated genre, who already care about performance-forward suspense and clean visual rules. This material rewards directors who like building tension through perception, blocking, and controlled reveals rather than pure spectacle.
director_appeal.detail: The ARC overlays, simulation bleed, and final live-op reveal give a director a chance to create a signature visual language without needing a giant effects canvas. It’s especially attractive to filmmakers who can stage action with clarity and make institutional spaces feel psychologically charged.

buyer_appeal.lane: Premium streamer thriller / theatrical-leaning espionage lane
buyer_appeal.detail: It can be packaged around one strong female lead and one strong male co-lead, so a buyer doesn’t need a giant ensemble or franchise IP to make it legible. The CIA/tech-paranoia hook, plus the contained training-facility backbone and international-op flavor, gives it exportable genre appeal with a clear trailer concept.

considerations.area: The opening is built on momentum, not mystery.
considerations.detail: The Istanbul sequence is a strong cold open, and the script smartly uses action to establish Walsh’s competence and the CIA’s pressure cooker. A next pass could keep the same propulsion while making sure the ARC premise lands as early as possible so the audience understands the movie’s true engine before page 20.

considerations.area: The final reveal has room to breathe.
considerations.detail: The cycle-reset ending is the movie’s biggest conceptual swing, and it already lands with force. One direction would be to slightly simplify the last stretch of reversals so the audience can absorb the emotional payoff of Ridley’s override before the next layer of reality arrives.

The script moves through Istanbul, Georgetown, The Farm, multiple simulated foreign cities, and a live D.C. climax. A production-friendly version could consolidate some of the international environments into fewer modular spaces without losing the sense that ARC can overwrite the world.

considerations.area: The ARC rules are strongest when they stay tactile.
considerations.detail: The card system, HUD prompts, and leaderboard logic are vivid because they are tied to choices the characters make in the room. A future pass could keep foregrounding the physical consequences of those prompts — who moves, who hesitates, who gets hurt — so the tech stays dramatic rather than explanatory.

considerations.area: Ridley and Ian carry the movie.
considerations.detail: The script is at its most magnetic when their relationship is both romantic and ideological, especially in the bar scene, the dojo, and the rooftop confrontation. One lever would be to keep protecting scenes where they test each other directly, because that’s where the concept becomes emotionally sticky.

considerations.area: The live-op climax justifies the scale.
considerations.detail: The switch from simulation to real-world D.C. gives the movie a clean escalation and a satisfying release of the premise. That also helps the package, because buyers can see exactly where the budget is going and why the third act earns it.
